# OmaCar — Roadmap

*Half of this document is written by a person and half is generated by
`omacar roadmap`. The generated half is clearly marked, and it exists because
the countable parts of a roadmap are the parts that go quietly wrong. The list
of everything a car owner and their agent would want to do with a car lives in
[doc/capabilities.json](capabilities.json), and is counted into the generated
half rather than retyped here.*

## The goal

> "A living roadmap that is extensive and covers eventually all aspects of a
> car and what a user and agent would want to do with their car. The goal is
> to build this as a highly effective tool, app, framework that is malleable,
> which fits into the Omarchy vision, and opens up possibilities for many
> people who otherwise would have never had these opportunities. This saves
> people from dumping thousands of dollars into old Snap-on tablets, OBD
> readers that are crap, and expensive mechanic visits just to get a code
> read."
>
> — the owner, 2026-09-28

**Make the best vehicle tool in the world free, make it run on a laptop
somebody already owns, and make it something their agent can extend.**

### Who it is for

- **The owner of an ordinary or older car** who has a warning light, a laptop
  and no idea what the light means, and who is about to pay somebody to find
  out.
- **The home mechanic** who does their own oil and brakes, and pays a shop for
  the jobs that need a scan tool for ninety seconds.
- **The enthusiast** reverse-engineering their own car, who wants the data the
  manufacturer never published.
- **The independent technician** who is tired of paying to catch up after
  falling behind on a subscription.
- **Their agents.** An owner who has Claude Code, Codex or another agent on
  the machine should be able to point it at the car and have it do real work,
  safely. That is a new kind of user, and it is a first-class one here.

### What it replaces, at today's prices

Every figure in this section is in the claims list in the generated block,
with the page it came from, the day it was read (2026-09-28), and how to check
it again. The one figure that could not be verified is marked as unverified.
The argument does not depend on the exact numbers. It depends on the ratio,
which is not close.

- **Scan tablets.** Snap-on's flagship ZEUS+ lists at $11,792, and keeping it
  current is $1,235 a year; even their entry MT2600 is $1,895. Autel's own
  store sells the MaxiSYS Ultra S2 at $6,499 and the mid-range MS906 Pro at
  $1,569, and Launch's X431 PAD VII Elite is $2,499. Every one of them is a
  mid-range tablet in a rubber case, running software, talking to the car over
  the same standard connector a $50 adapter uses.
- **Cheap readers.** A basic handheld reader is about $24 and a Bluetooth
  ELM327 clone roughly $6 to $17 (that range is unverified; see the claims).
  They read the engine's codes and little else, and the clones commonly copy
  old firmware and report a version they are not, so they fail in ways that
  look like the car's fault.
- **The shop.** RepairPal puts a check-engine diagnosis at $125 to $183 in
  labour, and O'Reilly says a shop charges around $100 just to read the codes.
  Parts stores read codes for free, which gives you the code and not the
  diagnosis, and the diagnosis is the part people are paying for.

OmaCar is the laptop you already own, a wired adapter (OBDLink's EX is $69.95
and the SX this was developed on $49.95), and software that costs nothing.

You are not paying Snap-on for the tablet. You are paying for **coverage**:
thousands of engineer-years spent working out what identifier means what on
which model. That is the moat, and it is the only real one. This document is
about how a free tool, and a community of owners and their agents, takes it.

---

## The governing principle: the owner decides

> "At the end of the day, it's whatever the owner of the car wants, regardless
> of anything else. The gospel is what the owner wants, with the caveat of the
> app and/or agent ensuring that the user is made aware of certain things or
> risks associated with any decisions that may require further guidance or
> thinking."
>
> — the owner, 2026-09-28

This sits above every other principle on this page. **The owner decides. The
app and the agent inform, warn and explain the risk before acting, and then do
what the owner chose.** It is already how the dangerous parts of OmaCar behave:
writes are disarmed until the owner arms them, every write states its
consequence before it is sent, and entering god mode says in as many words that
it is the owner's car and the owner's right.

It changes how every other rule here is read. A refusal is no longer a matter
of this project's taste. A refusal has to be one the owner has agreed to, and
it has to say why. Everything else the tool guards against becomes a warning:
the risk is stated, and the owner can accept it and go ahead.

The refusals and the warnings are also recorded as data, in the `refusals` and
`warnings` lists of [doc/capabilities.json](capabilities.json).
`omacar roadmap --check` fails if this section and that data disagree. It also
fails if `lib/modes.py` refuses anything the owner has not decided on, and if
the map plans a capability behind a confirmed refusal.

### The three refusals the owner has confirmed (2026-09-28)

These stay refusals whatever mode the tool is in and whatever the owner
accepts. The owner confirmed each as an exception to "the owner decides" on
2026-09-28. In his words, the first two are "obvious and necessary".

1. **Writes that disable emissions controls.** This is federal law, not a
   preference: Clean Air Act §203(a)(3) prohibits rendering an emission control
   inoperative, and EPA's 2020 enforcement policy says that covers software.
   The refusal is in `lib/modes.py`. It names the range it knows, and it says
   plainly that the list cannot be complete.
2. **Reprogramming that needs a manufacturer-signed image.** This tool cannot
   produce one. An interrupted transfer leaves a module with no firmware at
   all, which means a tow truck rather than a fault code. This is a technical
   impossibility for this tool, not a judgement about the owner.
3. **Writes to the car while it is moving.** The risk falls on other people on
   the road, who did not choose it. No mode, warning or plugin unlocks a write
   or an actuation while the car moves.

### The guards that become warnings (decided 2026-09-28)

These refuse in the code today. The owner decided that each becomes a warning
he can accept, with the risk stated first, and never silently. Until the
`safe.accept-risk` capability lands, the code keeps refusing them. The map
says so rather than pretending otherwise.

- **Guessing a routine identifier.** The risk: a routine is something a
  module *runs*, so a guessed number can spin a fan, cycle an ABS pump or
  retract a parking brake with a wheel off. The map plans it as
  `disc.routine-guess`, parked only, after the risk is accepted.
- **Writing or sweeping below 12.2 V.** The risk: a long session on a low
  battery can trip warning lights (a 25-minute key-on sweep tripped the ABS
  warning, which is why the floor exists) or leave the car unable to start.
- **An agent raising its own tier, promoting its own finding, or sending a
  write.** The risk: an agent can be wrong with confidence, and a finding it
  promotes itself becomes data other owners trust. Until accepted, an agent
  queues a proposal and the owner runs it or declines it.
- **Plugins breaking the driving-screen rules.** The risk: text entry, small
  targets and motion on a screen in view of the driver take attention off the
  road. Writes while moving stay refused whatever is accepted (see
  [Plugin safety rules](#plugin-safety-rules)).

## Why this is winnable

Five asymmetries. The third is the whole strategy, and the fifth is new.

**1. The hardware advantage is gone.** The compute in these tablets is weaker
than the second-hand laptop this was developed on. The interface is an ELM327
or STN chipset in an adapter costing tens of dollars. There is nothing in the
box worth four figures.

**2. Their software is worse than it should be.** These are single-vendor
codebases under decade-old assumptions, with no plugin story, no scripting and
no way to open them up. Data lands in a proprietary format on a device that
stops getting updates when the vendor decides. That is the same trap this
project was started to escape.

**3. Coverage is expensive per vendor and nearly free per community.**
Sweeping the full manufacturer identifier range takes about **70 minutes per
car**, but only **once per model** if the result is shared. Snap-on pays
engineers to do this behind closed doors, once per make, and rents it back. A
community does it in parallel, for free, and every owner of that model inherits
it. **A hundred CR-Z owners running one sweep each is a coverage database no
vendor can price against, because their cost floor is salaries and ours is
zero.** Some of that sharing already exists in public: OBDb publishes signal
sets for hundreds of models, and OmaCar reads them as leads.

**4. We can be honest in ways a product with a price tag cannot.** A tool that
must justify a subscription has an incentive to look confident. This one can
label a guess a guess, say "this came from cache", and refuse to show a number
it did not measure.

**5. The owner's agent is a new kind of user, and the incumbents are not
building for it.** A scan tablet is a closed appliance. Nobody's agent can
read its data, extend its screens or reason over a year of its logs. OmaCar
already hands the car to an agent over MCP, with the same gates a person has,
and this roadmap is machine-readable so an agent can pick up the next piece of
work itself. The owner who cannot write software but has an agent that can is
the person the incumbents' pricing locked out, and the person this project can
reach.

### What we do not pretend

Being credible means naming what is genuinely hard, gated or off the table.

- **Repair information** (ALLDATA, Mitchell1, wiring diagrams, OEM procedures)
  is licensed content. We will never clone it. We can link out, and we can let
  people attach their own notes to a vehicle. **Labour-time and valuation
  data** are licensed too: without a source it can cite, OmaCar explains and
  does not price.
- **Immobiliser and key programming** requires OEM security algorithms, is
  region-regulated, and is the single most abused capability in this market.
  It is out of scope, deliberately, and not a coverage gap we intend to close.
- **ECU reflashing** needs manufacturer-signed images and, in most markets now,
  an OEM subscription plus a J2534 device. It is one of the confirmed
  refusals above.
- **Security gateways** (FCA SGW, and equivalents spreading across other makes)
  require authenticated access to write to a modern vehicle at all. Read access
  is often unaffected. Where a gateway blocks us, we say so plainly rather than
  looking broken.
- **ADAS calibration** needs physical targets and a level floor. Software alone
  cannot do it.
- **Oscilloscope and multimeter work** needs hardware we do not ship. We can
  integrate with things people already own.
- **Not everything with a radio can be heard.** The owner's tyre sensors have
  no decoder in `rtl_433` today. A capture decides whether they can be heard,
  not a wish.

Everything else these tools do is reachable.

---

## The Omarchy fit

OmaCar is built to live on an Omarchy machine: it installs into the menu, puts
the car in the bar, can wear the desktop's theme, and answers Omarchy's agents
through `share/context.d/60-omacar`. The reimagining under way keeps that and
goes further in two directions.

**Agents are first-class users.** Every agent on the machine already knows
what car is plugged in, with nothing that identifies the owner. `omacar mcp`
gives an agent the car as tools, with the same gates a person has. The voice
assistant can move the screen, and cannot reach the bus. Next, the agent
framework gives an owner's agent a documented contract to build against: typed
car data, the design tokens, the driving state and declared permissions. With
that, the agent can build what this project never will: a screen for one car,
a data source for one model, a camera view for one mount.

**The tool is a framework that people's agents extend.** Profiles, reset
definitions and owner procedures are data files anyone can add to. Plugins add
commands, screens and hooks without forking. The capability map below tells an
agent what exists, what is next and what each piece needs. The Omarchy
ecosystem has its own plugins too: first-party ones in
`/usr/share/omarchy/shell/plugins`, and a community directory the Omarchy
manual points authors to. Bringing those into the car, in the car's look and
under the car's safety rules, is a domain of its own
([Plugin safety rules](#plugin-safety-rules)).

---

## Principles

**The governing principle is that the owner decides**, and the app and the
agent inform and warn before acting (above). The rest are load-bearing
underneath it, and several were learned by breaking something.

1. **Reads are free; writes are armed.** Writing is a first-class capability,
   not a hidden one: a tool that cannot clear a code after you fixed the fault
   is a viewer. But writes disarm themselves, refuse while the car is moving,
   and state their consequences before sending. Below 12.2 V they refuse
   today, and they will warn instead once the owner can accept the risk.
2. **Reprogramming stays out.** 0x34/0x36/0x37 need a manufacturer-signed image
   we cannot produce, and a partial transfer leaves a module unable to boot.
   Confirmed by the owner as an exception on 2026-09-28.
3. **No build step.** ES modules from disk, Python stdlib where possible. A
   tool you cannot open and repair is the trap it was built to replace.
4. **Never invent data.** A candidate is labelled a candidate. A cached scan
   says so. A tile the car cannot fill says "Not on this car", never zero. A
   price in this document names its page and the day it was read.
5. **Refuse when it matters, and say why.** Every guard names the incident
   that caused it. Under the governing principle, "when it matters" is the
   owner's call, and on 2026-09-28 he settled it: law, impossibility, and risk
   to people on the road who did not choose it. Everything else is a warning
   that states the risk, which the owner can accept.
6. **The car is not urgent work.** Everything in the background runs
   `Nice=10`. An unthrottled poll loop crashed the compositor on a 2-core
   machine once already.
7. **Your data is yours, in a format you can read.** SQLite and JSON on your
   own disk. No account is required, ever.
8. **Agents are users, not a feature.** Anything a person can do has an agent
   path through the same gates. An agent proposes and the owner decides, and
   an agent can never award itself more trust than it was given.
9. **Glanceable while moving.** Whatever is on screen while the car moves,
   ours or a plugin's, follows one set of rules by default: few numbers, big
   targets, no text entry and nothing new in motion. The owner can accept a
   warning to relax those. Writes stay greyed out with the reason, and that
   cannot be relaxed.
10. **No server of ours.** Sharing is a git repository, sync is between the
    owner's own machines over their own tailnet, and Work relays through the
    owner's own box. This follows the owner's decision of 2026-09-28 against
    cloud hosting for Work.
11. **Honest hardware advice.** Every price is dated and sourced, the guide
    says what cheap hardware cannot do, and it never recommends something
    nobody has run without saying so.

## Where we are

One vehicle has been validated end to end: a 2015 Honda CR-Z, on real hardware,
over a real adapter, across multi-leg days of driving. How much code there is,
how many tests pass, how much of the capability map has shipped, and how far
coverage has actually got are generated below rather than typed here, for the
reason given there.

The tool is broad already. It has live data, full scans filed as reports, codes
explained, readiness and Mode 06 with margins, a watchdog that captures
evidence while it happens, replay, a service book, a document library, a
garage, discovery that runs itself, validation by correlation, an MCP server,
an advisor that cites its evidence, plugins, and a phone screen waiting for a
dongle. The capability map lists each piece with the file that proves it.

**Honest limits**

- One validated vehicle profile, and no coverage for any other make.
- The manufacturer identifier space is barely touched even on that one car.
  The range actually swept is `0x0000`–`0x0FFF` out of `0x0000`–`0xA5FF`, and
  those sweeps ran before the resumable frontier existed, so the tool cannot
  yet *show* its own coverage and declines to quote a percentage it cannot
  prove. See doc/SWEEPING.md §5.
- On a real car a generic adapter reaches only the engine module, and the scan
  report says so rather than implying it read the airbag unit. Scanning every
  module is in Next.
- Pre-CAN support is written from the ELM327 datasheet and the ISO documents,
  and **has never been run against a pre-CAN car**.
- Nothing in `resets.json` or `procedures.json` is `verified` yet: verified
  means somebody ran it on a real car, and nobody has. That count is generated
  below, so the day it changes, this stops being said.
- **The interface is behind the engineering.** At the Omarchy meetup at
  Cloudflare HQ the verdict was that OmaCar was the strongest project shown
  *and* that its UI and UX needed a higher level of polish. Both halves are
  load-bearing. The foundation redesign in Now is the answer to the second
  half.
- **Living with it in a car is still being proven.** The screen now stays
  awake while the car moves. A tablet suspending mid-leg ended a drive on 8
  September, and the fix that makes preflight block on it is on
  `drive-day/hardening` and has not landed here yet.

## The capability map

**[doc/capabilities.json](capabilities.json) is the whole-car map:
everything an owner and their agent would want to do with a car, and where
OmaCar stands on each.** It is organised into domains, from fault codes and
smog prep to tyres, cameras, navigation, paperwork, the agent framework and
Omarchy plugins in the car. Each capability says what a person wants from it,
what their agent does with it, its status, its safety tier, the hardware it
needs, what it depends on, and the files that prove it. The generated block
below counts it by domain and status and lists everything that has shipped.

The map is honest by construction rather than by care. `omacar roadmap
--check` refuses a map in which:

- a `shipped` or `building` entry names no files, or names a file git does not
  track;
- a `shipped` entry depends on something that has not shipped;
- a dependency does not exist, or dependencies form a loop;
- a capability that writes to or moves the car does not name the
  `lib/modes.py` action that gates it;
- a capability is gated by a refusal the owner confirmed. Reprogramming
  cannot appear on the map even as a plan;
- a capability is gated by a guard the owner made a warning, such as guessing
  a routine, and is marked shipped while the code still refuses it;
- `lib/modes.py` refuses an action that neither the refusals nor the warnings
  record a decision on, or the governing principle above does not name a
  refusal or warning the data holds.

The check can prove that a file exists and is tracked. It cannot prove that
the file works on your car, and that is what each entry's notes are for: which
cars and adapters it has actually met.

**Adding to it.** Pick the domain, write the four sentences (title, user,
agent, notes), choose the status honestly, and read the code before writing
`shipped`. Name the gate if it touches the car, then run `omacar roadmap
--check`, which names every problem it finds. Never reuse an id.

**How an agent should use this roadmap.**

1. Run `omacar roadmap --list next`, or read `doc/capabilities.json`
   directly. Each `next` item is printed with the status of everything it
   depends on and the hardware it needs.
2. Pick one whose `depends` have all shipped and whose `needs` the owner has.
   If a dependency is not there yet, that dependency is the real next item.
3. Read its notes and evidence, then the design doc for its step in
   `doc/design/`. If there is none, write one first, in the house pattern:
   problem, shape, rejected approaches, design, rollout, open questions. Get
   the owner's decisions recorded in it before building.
4. Build on a branch, with tests listed in `test/all.sh` the day they are
   written. Add an `inflight` entry to `doc/roadmap.json` naming the file that
   will exist when it lands.
5. When it lands, move the capability's status, list its evidence, remove the
   `inflight` entry, and run `omacar roadmap`. Never write `shipped` for
   something that has not run.

The principles above bind an agent exactly as they bind a person. An agent
never states a number it cannot source. It does not mark its own finding
validated or send a write the owner has not approved. Those limits are
warnings the owner can accept with the risk stated, not refusals, and until
`safe.accept-risk` lands the code holds them. No agent writes to a moving car,
ever.

*A profile entry below `validated` may not drive a gauge. That rule
is enforced in code, not by convention, which is why the validated

Workshop definitions — **procedures**: 11 defined (11 reported); **resets**: 2 defined (2 reported).

`verified` means somebody ran it on a real car and it did what it
said. Until a definition carries that word it is `reported`, and the
app shows it as reported.

**Identifier space explored** — the manufacturer range is `0x0000`–`0xA5FF`, 42,496 identifiers per module per service.

No frontier record on the machine that generated this. That is not
the same as nothing having been swept — early sweeps on the CR-Z ran
before the resumable frontier existed and left no record it can read.
It does mean the tool cannot currently *prove* a coverage percentage
to you, and so it declines to quote one.

On this machine: 1 vehicle database, 0 drive fault-log sessions, 0 candidate correlation logs, 0 learned module maps. Counts only — the field log below is the place for what those drives actually were.

unverifiable claim is visibly marked as one instead of sitting in
the prose looking like a measurement.

**Field log** — the car, and the world, not the repository

Nothing in a checkout knows a car was driven or a demo was given, so
this half is hand-appended to `doc/roadmap.json` and rendered here. A
journal is the one form of hand-maintained document that does not rot:
when somebody stops keeping it, it stops. It does not start lying.

Protocol identified as ISO 15765-4 (CAN 29/500), the two hybrid controllers found awake on 29-bit headers, and -- after service 0x22 came back empty across thousands of identifiers -- the service 0x19 fault catalogues found, which is where the Honda-specific data actually was.

## Plugin safety rules

Omarchy plugins and OmaCar's own plugins will reach the car's screen. A drive
has to look like one product and has to be as safe as OmaCar's own screens,
whoever wrote the plugin. These rules are enforced **by the app, not requested
of the plugin**. Today OmaCar's own screens follow them. Nothing yet enforces
them on a plugin; that is the `oplug.safety-rules` capability, and it is in
Next with the plugin contract. The contract supports Omarchy's full-screen
`panel` kind first (approved 2026-09-28).

Rule 5 is a refusal: writes to the car while it is moving are one of the three
refusals the owner confirmed on 2026-09-28, and nothing a plugin declares or
an owner accepts unlocks it. Every other rule is a default. The owner can
relax it for a plugin after the app states the risk. That makes plugins
breaking the driving-screen rules a warning, not a refusal (decided
2026-09-28).

**While the car is moving:**

1. **Glanceable only.** A few values, large, readable in under a second. There
   are no lists to scroll and no dense text.
2. **No text entry.** No keyboards and no search fields. Voice is the only
   input that asks nothing of the driver's eyes.
3. **Targets a thumb can hit.** At least 48 px, and 56 px on a coarse pointer,
   the same floor as OmaCar's own tokens.
4. **Nothing new in motion.** Values may change. Nothing slides in, pulses or
   animates for its own sake, and effects pause.
5. **Writes and actuation are greyed out, with the reason.** A plugin reaches
   the car only through the same gates a person does: `lib/modes.py`, the write
   arm and the motion check. There is no side door, and this rule has no
   override.
6. **Every number says where it came from.** A plugin that draws a reading
   carries its source, like OmaCar's tiles, and draws words rather than a zero
   when it has no value.

**Always:**

7. **A plugin declares what it needs**: which tier, which data, and whether it
   runs code. The server enforces the declaration, and `omacar plugins` shows
   it before the owner relies on it.
8. **Installing, configuring and rearranging happen parked.**
9. **It wears the active look.** A plugin uses the design tokens and type it
   is given, so the car looks like one thing.
10. **There is no sandbox yet, and we say so.** An Omarchy plugin is QML that
    runs inside the shell's own process, and an OmaCar plugin's command runs
    as the owner. A review checklist can catch careless plugins but not
    hostile ones. Isolating web views on their own origin is research, not a
    promise.

Under the governing principle the owner can install whatever they like, and
relax any rule above except rule 5 once the risk is stated. What the app will
not do is let any plugin write to or move the car while it is moving.

### Next

In this order, which is the owner's.

**1. IMA and Honda data: the 2026-09-29 discovery drives.** Asymmetry 3
claims that coverage is expensive per vendor and nearly free per community.
This is that claim being run for the first time, on one car, by one person. It
is worth stating exactly how far it has got, including the parts that did not
work.

*What is known, from this car's own captures.* Both hybrid controllers answer
on 29-bit headers: `18DA03F1`, which `lib/discover.py` labels *hybrid /
battery*, and `18DA04F1`, labelled *hybrid / motor*. Those labels are the
repo's own and are as far as the evidence goes. Service `0x19` subfunction
`0x0A` (*list every fault you are capable of setting*) returns a catalogue of
49 codes from the first and 26 from the second, byte-identical across three
separate drive logs. That catalogue is the prize so far: a map of what Honda
built each module to measure. What it measures can be guessed from the code
numbers, but that guess is a reading, not a lookup, and only two of these codes
have a description anywhere in this repository. No generic scan tool shows the
catalogue at all. The hybrid screen now shows it, with the caveat below leading
rather than footnoted.

*What is routinely misread.* Every one of the 263 status observations captured
so far carries status byte `0x40`, `testNotCompletedThisOperationCycle`. The
correct sentence is "these monitors have not run since the last clear", not
"this car has eighteen hybrid faults". Getting it wrong frightens somebody
about a healthy car, which is the exact failure a free tool has no excuse for.

*What is a dead end, and precisely how far.* Service `0x22` answers on both
hybrid modules only in the ISO 14229 identification block `F100`–`F19F`. The
range actually swept, `0x0000`–`0x0FFF`, is empty, which is true of that range
and not of the space: about nine tenths of it has never been asked.

*What is not known.* Whether service `0x21`, the pre-UDS live-data service and
the most likely home for a live state of charge on a 2015 Honda, answers at
all: the only sweep on record used an 11-bit header on a 29-bit car. Whether
any identifier exists above `0x0FFF`. Whether either module stores snapshot
records, which would be Honda's own byte layout with a fault name attached.
Whether IMA control traffic reaches the OBD connector at all.

*What has never been captured.* No live IMA quantity of any kind: no state of
charge, pack voltage, pack current, battery temperature, assist, regeneration
or cell balance. Until that changes the app shows no hybrid gauge, and the
profile format enforces that.

*The drives, in order.* First read `ATRV` with the engine running, parked and
the handbrake on. Recapture the catalogues with raw payloads kept. Sweep
`0x21` across all four known headers with the engine idling, so a byte tracking
charge or current has something to vary against. Ask generic PID `0x5B` once,
because it is in this car's own supported bitmap and has never been polled.
Then extend `0x22` past `0x0FFF` in short bursts via `omacar discover`. **No
long key-on-engine-off sweep**: a 25-minute one tripped the ABS warning, which
is why the voltage floor exists. Scanning the CR-Z's known modules for faults
belongs to the same work, so Vehicle's systems list is true on the real car
and not only on the simulator.

*Why this is the strategy and not a hobby.* The catalogue is already a
shareable artifact with provenance, so the second CR-Z owner does not repeat
any of it. The procedure is model-shaped rather than Honda-shaped. If it works
on the CR-Z, the moat in the opening argument is not knowledge. It is only that
nobody had shared it.

**2. Service resets, per make.** These run after the IMA drives (decided
2026-09-28). They are the resets that most often force a shop visit: oil life
over the bus, electronic parking brake service mode, steering angle
calibration, battery registration, throttle and idle relearn, and diesel
particulate regeneration. The routine-control path and the definition format
already exist, and only two generic clears are defined. Every definition is
per make and starts `unverified` until somebody runs it on a real car. None is
found by guessing, since guessing a routine becomes a separate, risk-accepted
act. The old roadmap called this the highest-value item per hour of work.

**3. Navigation and GPS, offline.** Decided with the owner on 2026-09-27/28:
MapLibre with Protomaps tiles for the map, Valhalla for routing and Piper for
spoken directions, all running on the tablet. Piper is not bundled. It is
installed as a normal system package and run as its own program, and its
active repository is GPL-3.0. Voice clips rendered ahead of time are just
audio files. Position comes from a u-blox NEO-M9V receiver with a roof
antenna, which also dead-reckons through tunnels. GNSS speed also becomes a
trusted yardstick for validating discovered data. Location history arrives
with retention the owner controls, not after it.

**4. Tyre pressures by radio.** The owner's Tymate TM2 sensors broadcast
pressure and temperature on 433.92 MHz, and `rtl_433` has no Tymate decoder
today. The next step: once the RTL-SDR radio arrives, the owner spends about
an hour recording the sensors with `rtl_433`'s generic and flex decoders.
Buying sensors `rtl_433` already supports is the fallback, only if that fails.
Nothing is sent to the car. If the recording decodes, Home's single tyre
callout becomes four, as the foundation design anticipated.

**5. The agent framework.** It is an SDK so owners' agents can build solutions
for their own cars: car data, CarPlay, the interface, cameras and navigation.
It covers a documented contract, a scaffold that starts a plugin with its test,
permissions a plugin declares and the server enforces, and more events to hook.
The Omarchy plugin contract and the plugin safety rules are part of the same
work, because a car screen from an Omarchy plugin and a car screen from an
owner's agent are the same problem. The contract supports Omarchy's
full-screen `panel` kind first.

**6. The hardware guide, especially for older cars.** It says which adapter
for which car and protocol, what a clone cannot do, how to power a tablet
without a fire risk, how to fit the GNSS antenna, and what of a Snap-on kit
carries over. Every price is dated and sourced.

**7. Onboarding, for users and for agents, on Omarchy.** For a person, it goes
from "I have a car and a laptop" to a first useful answer in minutes. For an
agent, it is one guide to the principles, the tiers, the MCP tools, this
roadmap and how to test.

**8. Looks and the car in 3D.** Looks become folders (palette, logo and
texture), with the owner's chrome and carbon-fibre logos. An optional 3D model
of the owner's own car can replace the picture, and the viewer for it already
exists. Honda-badged art stays in the private assets folder, out of git.

**9. Recalls by VIN.** It checks the decoded VIN against NHTSA's free public
recall data and cites the result. The VIN decode already asks NHTSA, so this
is small. Moved into Next on 2026-09-28.

### Later

Wanted, and sequenced after everything in Next. The map holds the full list.
The larger pieces are:

- **Work**: coding sessions on the owner's Omarchy machines from the car, on
  his Claude subscription, relayed through his own box with no cloud hosting,
  and voice-only while driving. It comes after the Next items, then OmaMenu
  (decided 2026-09-28).
- **OmaMenu**, a system-wide replacement for the Omarchy menu.
- **Warnings the owner can accept** (`safe.accept-risk`): turning routine
  guessing, the voltage floor, the agent limits and the plugin driving rules
  from refusals into warnings, as decided on 2026-09-28. Until it lands the
  code still refuses all four.
- **Every module on more makes**, and the transports that open them: J2534,
  SocketCAN, and the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi adapters people already own.
- **Omarchy plugins in the car**, beyond the contract: a theming bridge, car
  versions of existing plugins, a review checklist and an install flow.
- **Professional parity**: gateway handling where it is legitimately possible,
  scope integration, and fleet use for a small business.
- **Beyond parity**: predictive alerts from your own history, the car's record
  synced to your own machines, and cranking-voltage trends.

### Research

Nobody knows yet whether these can be done well: IMA cell balance, reading
body states, crash detection with a consented message, reading messages
aloud, valuation without licensed data, comparing your car against others like
it without a server, an advisor that works with no signal, which Omarchy
plugins can work in a car, and sandboxing plugins at all.

## What changed from the old phases, and why

| Old | Now | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **1.1** Service resets | Next, after the IMA drives; framework building | The routine path and the format exist, and there are no per-make definitions yet. Moved into Next by the owner on 2026-09-28. |
| **1.1b** Owner procedures | Shipped | Unchanged. |
| **1.2** Bi-directional test UI | Building | The screen exists with a live trace. On a real car only a validated actuator reaches a button, and no car has one yet. |
| **1.3** Live data | Shipped | Snapshot-on-trigger was listed as "not yet". It shipped: the watchdog freezes a full snapshot when a rule fires. |
| **1.4** Guided diagnosis | Shipped | The advisor's `code`, `symptom` and `recording` answers, which cite their evidence. |
| **1.5** Reports | Shipped | A printable report and a self-contained file to hand over. |
| **1.6**, **1.7** | Shipped | Unchanged. |
| **1.8** The interface, as a feature | Now | It became the foundation redesign. |
| **2.1**–**2.3** | Shipped | Unchanged. |
| **2.4** Cross-model inference | Later | It needs a second model's data first. |
| **2.5** Protocol breadth | Building | Written and never run on a pre-CAN car. |
| **2.6** Honda IMA | Next, first | The 2026-09-29 drives. |
| **Phase 3** OmaCar Cloud (Rails) | Dropped as a hosted service | See below. |
| **Phase 4** Professional parity | Later | Unchanged in substance, behind the owner's own car. |
| **Phase 5** Past parity | Split | The plugin API shipped and automation was always the CLI. Predictive alerts are Later, a local model is Research, and hands-free use grew into voice and Work. |

**Why there is no OmaCar Cloud.** Phase 3 proposed a Rails service for pooled
discovery, garages that outlive a reinstall, fleet-wide battery comparisons and
shareable report links. It said it would "never be a dependency". Two things
since then make it unnecessary as well as unwanted:

- **The pool did not need a server.** `lib/pool.py` does pooled discovery over
  a git repository. Fetching is an HTTP GET, contributing is a pull request,
  and a club can run its own. There are no accounts and no uptime.
- **The owner decided against cloud hosting on 2026-09-28**, for Work. The
  relay runs on his own box. The same reasoning applies to everything else
  Phase 3 wanted.

So each part goes somewhere a server is not:

- Pooled discovery shipped over git.
- Garages that outlive a reinstall become sync between the owner's own machines
  over their own tailnet (Later).
- Shareable reports are a file, which already exists, rather than a link that
  dies with a service.
- Comparing a car against others of its model and age is still wanted, and it
  moves to Research. Without a server it needs an opt-in way to share that
  identifies nobody, and nobody has designed that yet.

Principle 10 records the decision.

---

## How we will know it is working

Not downloads. These:

1. **Vehicles with a validated community profile.** The only number that
   matters. It is counted for you in the generated block, so it can never be
   rounded up.
2. **Makes with any coverage at all.** Breadth of the long tail.
3. **A repair somebody completed** that would otherwise have been a shop
   visit.
4. **A professional technician using it in a paid job.** The real threshold.
5. **Time from plugging into an unknown car to useful manufacturer data.**
   Today it is roughly 70 minutes of sweeping. The target is *seconds*,
   because somebody else already did it.
6. **Something an owner's agent built for their car that we did not.** The
   test of the framework is work nobody here planned.
7. **Capabilities that moved to shipped with evidence.** Counted in the
   generated block, which refuses to count one that names no tracked file.

---

## Decided with the owner (2026-09-28)

The questions this roadmap could not settle from the repository, and the
owner's answers. Each has changed the capability map and the text above.

1. **Refusals and warnings.** Writes to the car while it is moving join the
   emissions and signed-reprogramming refusals as a hard refusal. Routine
   guessing, the 12.2 V floor, the agent limits and the plugin driving rules
   become warnings the owner can accept, with the risk stated. See
   [the governing principle](#the-governing-principle-the-owner-decides).
2. **Service resets per make** move into Next, after the IMA drives.
3. **Recalls by VIN** move into Next.
4. **Work, then OmaMenu,** come after the Next items, in that order.
5. **Piper is not bundled.** It is installed as a normal system package and run
   as its own program, and its active repository is GPL-3.0. Voice clips
   rendered ahead of time are just audio files.
6. **Tymate tyre sensors.** Once the RTL-SDR arrives, the owner spends about an
   hour recording them with `rtl_433`'s generic and flex decoders. Buying
   supported sensors is the fallback, only if that fails.
7. **The plugin contract** supports Omarchy's full-screen `panel` kind first.
8. **The three-button bar panel** is dropped from the in-flight list.
   Nobody could say what it was for. It dates from the first generated
   roadmap on 2026-09-03, where 1.8 asked for "a bar panel that says three
   things instead of thirty".

---

## The one-sentence version

*A second-hand laptop, a cheap cable, a community that shares what it finds,
and an agent that works for the owner should be able to out-diagnose a tool
costing a hundred times as much. Every model somebody maps makes it true for
one more car.*
